posts.raw_content:
Japanese prosecutors are seeking nine years in prison for a 37-year-old farmer who admitted setting fire to a mosque in Hokkaido – a building that had itself previously been declared illegally constructed by local authorities.

Ryotaro Ishii, a farmer from Chitose, appeared before the Sapporo District Court on September 24 and admitted to the charges against him, telling the court there was “no mistake” about the allegations. Prosecutors requested a nine-year custodial sentence, while the defense argued for a substantially shorter term. A verdict is scheduled for October 29.

The case concerns a prefabricated building used as an Islamic mosque in Kakuyama, Ebetsu, which was owned by a company operated by a Pakistani man. Ishii was accused of setting the building on fire in February, completely destroying it.

However, the mosque had already been the subject of a long-running dispute with Ebetsu authorities.

The building stood inside an urbanization-control area, where construction is heavily restricted. Ebetsu City previously confirmed that it discovered the mosque during a September 2021 inspection and subsequently determined that it did not comply with Japan’s City Planning Act. The city classified it as an illegal structure and issued corrective guidance.

Reporting following the fire similarly stated that the mosque had been built without the required permission and that Ebetsu had issued corrective administrative guidance in September and October 2025.

None of that made destroying the building legal, and prosecutors have argued that Ishii’s motivation went considerably beyond a dispute over building regulations.

According to Kyodo, prosecutors said Ishii had developed resentment toward foreigners after becoming unhappy with the behavior of foreign nationals who visited to purchase agricultural equipment. Prosecutors accused him of using a self-serving sense of justice to justify the arson in an attempt to drive Pakistanis out of Japan.

Ishii testified that foreigners had previously entered the farm where he worked without permission and that he regularly watched online videos criticizing Pakistanis. The day before the arson, his chainsaw disappeared, and Ishii said he assumed foreigners had stolen it:

    “I got angry and thought I’d teach them a lesson.” 

Ishii described what he did as essentially “taking it out on them” and told the court he now believes he had done something terrible. HTB reports that he also testified that he had thought, “I’ll drive the Pakistanis out of this country.”

The charges extend beyond the destruction of the mosque. According to HTB, Ishii is accused of setting fires at a mosque and other premises operated by Pakistanis using plastic bottles containing gasoline. Prosecutors said the incidents caused more than ¥20 million in combined damage and argued that the circumstances suggested a degree of planning.

His defense disputes that characterization, arguing that the attacks were not planned and that Ishii was not acting as an ideological offender. His lawyers contend that the likelihood of him committing another similar offense is low and have asked the court to impose a sentence shorter than the prosecution’s requested nine years.

The case also comes amid wider tensions surrounding the Pakistani community in Ebetsu. Roughly 200 Pakistani nationals were reported to be living in the city in late 2025, many working in used-car dismantling and exports. Local reporting documented disputes over illegal buildings in the area’s urbanization-control zone, alongside online claims about the community.

Whether prosecutors receive the full nine-year sentence they have requested will be decided when the Sapporo District Court delivers its verdict on October 29.
